## Effort trends {#effort}

### Total fishing days by year and country (AER, all gears) {#effort-country}

Total fishing effort of the EU fleets in the study area changed from `r fmt_n(eff_eu_first)` days in `r aer_years_start` to `r fmt_n(eff_eu_last)` days in `r aer_years_end`, a change of `r fmt_pct(eff_eu_change_pct)` over the period (Figure \@ref(fig:aer-effort-country-total)). Over the years in which UK effort data are available, the fishing effort of all fleets changed from `r fmt_n(eff_all_first)` fishing days in `r aer_years_start` to `r fmt_n(eff_all_ukend)` in `r aer_uk_years_end` (`r fmt_pct(eff_all_change_pct)`; `r aer_uk_years_end` was also affected by the COVID-19 pandemic). Between `r aer_years_start` and `r aer_uk_years_end`, France contributed `r fmt_pct(share_fra)` of the AER fishing days, the UK `r fmt_pct(share_gbr)` and all other countries together `r fmt_pct(share_oth)`. No UK effort data are available for the years after Brexit.

```{r aer-effort-country-total, fig.height=6, fig.cap=cap[["aer-effort-country-total"]]}

# Stacking order from the bottom up; all other countries are grouped as "Other"
stack_order <- c("FRA", "NLD", "DEU", "BEL", "Other", "GBR")

effort_cty <- 
  aer_effort_summary |>
  filter(sub_reg %in% study_divisions_aer,
         year    <= aer_years_end) |>
  mutate(country_code = if_else(country_code %in% stack_order, country_code, "Other")) |>
  group_by(year, country_code) |>
  summarise(totfishdays = sum(totfishdays, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  complete(year = aer_years_start:aer_years_end,
           country_code = stack_order,
           fill = list(totfishdays = NA_real_)) |>
  mutate(country_code = factor(country_code, levels = stack_order))

# effort_cty %>% filter(year >= 2015, year <= 2020) %>%  group_by(country_code) %>% 
#   summarise(totfishdays = sum(totfishdays, na.rm=TRUE)) %>% 
#   ungroup() %>% 
#   mutate(pct = totfishdays / sum(totfishdays, na.rm=TRUE)) %>% 
#   print()

# effort_cty %>% 
#   filter(country_code != "GBR") %>%  
#   group_by(year) %>%
#   summarise(totfishdays = sum(totfishdays, na.rm=TRUE)) %>%
#   ungroup() 

# effort_cty %>% 
#   filter(year <= 2020) %>%  
#   group_by(country_code, year) %>%
#   summarise(totfishdays = sum(totfishdays, na.rm=TRUE)) %>%
#   ungroup() %>% 
#   View()


# Years without UK data: asterisk above the total of that year
gbr_missing <- effort_cty |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(total   = sum(totfishdays, na.rm = TRUE),
            gbr_na  = all(is.na(totfishdays[country_code == "GBR"]) |
                          totfishdays[country_code == "GBR"] == 0),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(gbr_na)

ggplot(effort_cty, aes(x = year, y = totfishdays, fill = country_code)) +
  geom_col(position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE), width = 0.8, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_text(data = gbr_missing, aes(x = year, y = total, label = "*"),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, vjust = -0.2, size = 6,
            colour = "red", fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = flag_colours, drop = FALSE, na.value = "grey70",
                    name = "Country") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = aer_years_start:aer_years_end,
                     limits = c(aer_years_start - 0.5, aer_years_end + 0.5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.08)),
                     labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(title    = "AER: Fishing days by year and country",
       subtitle = paste0(study_area_lab, "  \u2014  All gears combined"),
       caption  = if (nrow(gbr_missing) > 0)
                    paste0("* No UK (GBR) effort data in ",
                           paste(range(gbr_missing$year), collapse = "\u2013"),
                           " (not in the AER after ", aer_uk_years_end, ")."),
       x = "Year", y = "Fishing days") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.x  = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
        legend.position = "bottom",
        plot.caption = element_text(size = 7, colour = "grey40")) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 1))
```

### Total fishing days by year, country and gear category (AER)

The breakdown of effort by gear category (Figure \@ref(fig:aer-effort-gear-cat)) shows which gears dominate the study area. The dominant gears were bottom trawl/seine, dredge, gillnet, pot/trap and Other/mixed. French bottom trawl/seine and gillnet effort has declined over time. French dredge effort also appears to decline, but this is partly offset by an increase in Other/mixed gear. The Dutch fleet is only visible in bottom trawl/seine and Other/mixed gear.


### Total fishing days by year, country and vessel length class (AER)

Fishing effort by vessel length class (Figure \@ref(fig:aer-effort-trend)) reveals distinct fleet structures by country. The French fleet dominated the 10–12 m and 12–18 m length classes. The UK and France both had a substantial share of the under-10 m effort. French effort declined gradually in the 18–24 m length class. The Dutch fleet was concentrated in the 24–40 m and >40 m classes with relatively stable effort. The 24–40 m length class showed the most multi-country competition (UK, French, Dutch and Belgian vessels).


### Fishing days by year, country, gear and vessel size (AER)

Figure \@ref(fig:aer-effort-gt) shows the effort by gear and vessel size together, which reveals the specialisation of the fleets. The French vessels dominated the bottom trawl/seine effort up to 24 m, with a strong reduction for French 18–24 m vessels. French dredge effort came mostly from vessels between 10 and 18 m. Dutch effort was concentrated in bottom trawl/seine (VL2440) and Other/mixed (VL40XX). Belgian vessels dominated beam trawl effort (VL1824 and VL2440).

### Disaggregation of bottom trawl/seine (FDI-derived) {#effort-split}

As described in Section \@ref(fdi-data), the AER Bottom trawl/seine category was disaggregated into conventional otter trawl (OTB/OTT/PTB) and seine (SSC/SDN) gears using proportional split keys derived from the STECF FDI Effort data. The left panel of Figure \@ref(fig:aer-split-trend) shows the absolute fishing days by gear type over `r aer_split_years_start`–`r aer_years_end`. The right panel shows the gear-type share based on direct FDI splits only: conventional otter trawl accounts for `r otb_share_range`% of the days, and seine (SSC/SDN) for `r seine_share_range`%. The picture varies strongly by country (Figure \@ref(fig:aer-split-fra-nld-bars)): France and the UK fish mostly with otter trawls, while the Netherlands fishes predominantly with seines, reflecting the Dutch flyshoot fleet. Of all seine days in the study area, `r fmt_pct(seine_pct("NLD"))` are Dutch, `r fmt_pct(seine_pct("FRA"))` French and `r fmt_pct(seine_pct("GBR"))` British. Note that BEL and DEU received pooled fallback splits due to sparse FDI coverage and are therefore excluded from the percentage panel.

```{r aer-split-trend, fig.height=6, fig.width=10, fig.cap=cap[["aer-split-trend"]]}

if (!is.null(aer_split)) {

  split_2colours <- c(
    "Bottom trawl (OTB/OTT/PTB)" = "#E15759",
    "Seine (SSC/SDN)"             = "#4E79A7"
  )

  # Years without any UK (GBR) effort data, over all gears
  gbr_missing_yr <- gbr_missing_years(aer_effort_summary)

  # ---- Left panel: absolute fishing days ---------------------------------------
  abs_data <- aer_split |>
    filter(year <= aer_years_end,
           gear_type != "Unsplit") |>
    group_by(year, gear_type) |>
    summarise(fishdays = sum(totfishdays_split, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(gear_type = factor(gear_type, levels = names(split_2colours)))

  abs_missing <- abs_data |>
    group_by(year) |>
    summarise(total = sum(fishdays), .groups = "drop") |>
    filter(year %in% gbr_missing_yr)

  p_abs <- ggplot(abs_data, aes(x = year, y = fishdays, fill = gear_type)) +
    geom_col(position = "stack", width = 0.8) +
    geom_text(data = abs_missing, aes(x = year, y = total, label = "*"),
              inherit.aes = FALSE, vjust = -0.2, size = 6,
              colour = "red", fontface = "bold") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = split_2colours, name = NULL,
                      guide = guide_legend(nrow = 1)) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(aer_split_years_start, aer_years_end, by = 2)) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.08)),
                       labels = scales::label_comma()) +
    labs(subtitle = "Absolute fishing days", x = "Year", y = "Fishing days") +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(axis.text.x   = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
          plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9, colour = "grey30"))

  # ---- Right panel: gear share (FDI direct splits only) -------------------------
  pct_data <- aer_split |>
    filter(year         %in% aer_split_years_start:aer_years_end,
           split_source == "FDI direct",
           gear_type    != "Unsplit") |>
    group_by(year, gear_type) |>
    summarise(totdays = sum(totfishdays_split, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    group_by(year) |>
    mutate(pct = round(100 * totdays / sum(totdays), 0)) |>
    ungroup() |>
    mutate(gear_type = factor(gear_type, levels = names(split_2colours)))

  pct_missing <- tibble::tibble(
    year = intersect(gbr_missing_yr, unique(pct_data$year))
  )

  p_pct <- ggplot(pct_data, aes(x = year, y = pct, colour = gear_type, group = gear_type)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
    geom_point(size = 3) +
    geom_text(aes(label = paste0(pct, "%")),
              vjust = -0.8, size = 2.8, show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_point(data = pct_missing, aes(x = year, y = 0),
               inherit.aes = FALSE, shape = 8, size = 1.8, stroke = 0.8,
               colour = "red") +
    scale_colour_manual(values = split_2colours, name = NULL) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(aer_split_years_start, aer_years_end, by = 2)) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100),
                       expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.08)),
                       labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1)) +
    coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
    labs(subtitle = "Gear share (%) \u2014 FDI direct splits only",
         x = "Year", y = "Share of fishing days (%)") +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(legend.position = "none",
          axis.text.x     = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
          plot.subtitle   = element_text(size = 9, colour = "grey30"))

  p_abs + p_pct +
    plot_layout(guides = "collect") +
    plot_annotation(
      title    = "AER \u2014 Bottom trawl/seine disaggregated by gear code",
      subtitle = paste0(study_area_lab, "  \u2014  FDI gear-code split applied to AER fishing days"),
      caption  = if (length(gbr_missing_yr) > 0)
                   paste0("* No UK (GBR) effort data in ",
                          paste(range(gbr_missing_yr), collapse = "\u2013"),
                          " (not in the AER after ", aer_uk_years_end, ")."),
      theme    = theme(
        plot.title      = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold"),
        plot.subtitle   = element_text(size = 9, colour = "grey30"),
        plot.caption    = element_text(size = 7, colour = "grey40"),
        legend.position = "bottom"
      )
    )

} else {
  cat("aer_split not available.\n")
}
```

### Total GFW fishing days by year and flag state {#gfw-effort}

GFW-derived fishing effort in the study area (Figure \@ref(fig:gfw-plot-flag-total)) shows a different trend from the AER data. The GFW effort showed a clear increasing trend, dominated by small vessels (S1 <100 GT), whose growing contribution drove much of the increase. This may partly reflect improving AIS coverage over time rather than a genuine increase in fishing activity.

The two data sources measure effort differently: AER reports administrative fishing days declared by Member States; GFW estimates fishing days from AIS vessel-tracking. Several factors can explain systematic differences between the two series:

- **Method for counting fishing days**: AER records one fishing day as any day on which a vessel is registered as fishing by its flag state; GFW counts a vessel-day as active when AIS-derived speed and movement patterns are classified as fishing behaviour. The two methods can disagree for the same vessel on the same day.
- **AIS coverage and adoption**: AIS was gradually mandated across the EU fleet between 2008 and 2014. Early years of the GFW series therefore under-represent vessels that did not yet carry AIS transponders, leading to lower GFW effort estimates before ~2014.
- **Small coastal vessels**: Vessels below ~15 m LOA are not required to carry AIS in many jurisdictions. This segment is captured in the AER (via logbook reporting) but largely absent from GFW, causing a structural undercount in GFW relative to AER for gears dominated by small vessels (e.g. pot/trap, gillnet).
- **Gear type assignment**: GFW classifies gear from registry information and AIS movement patterns; misclassification can shift effort between gear categories when comparing with AER gear-specific totals.
- **Spatial attribution**: AER effort is attributed to the ICES division declared in the logbook; GFW effort is attributed to the GPS position of the fishing event. In boundary areas the two can differ.


## Spatial patterns in fishing effort (GFW) {#gfw-spatial}

This section describes where fishing takes place in the eastern Channel, how the distribution of the main national fleets changed after Brexit, and how concentrated the fishing effort is. It is based on the GFW data, which mainly represent the larger vessels that carry AIS (Section \@ref(gfw-data)).

### Spatial distribution of fishing events {#gfw-events}

Although the GFW data cannot be used as an indicator of total fishing effort, the spatial distributions can still be used to assess the spatial patterns in the fishing operations. Figure \@ref(fig:gfw-plot-spatial-all) shows a sample of all fishing events, coloured by country, and Figure \@ref(fig:gfw-plot-spatial-by-year) the same per year. The French effort was spread broadly with stronger concentrations in the Baie de Seine and Pas de Calais. UK effort was concentrated in the northern part of 27.7.d and Dutch effort was mostly concentrated in the central-eastern part of 27.7.d.


The kernel density maps (Figure \@ref(fig:gfw-plot-kde)) convert the fishing event locations into a continuous surface of effort intensity, normalised within each year (Section \@ref(gfw-data)). This makes the annual maps comparable in terms of spatial pattern, but means that absolute effort levels cannot be compared between years: a year with low total effort and a year with high total effort will both have cells reaching 1.0. The Baie de Seine and Pas de Calais consistently showed the highest effort densities, reflecting the concentration of bottom trawl and dredge activities.

### Spatial distribution before and after Brexit {#brexit}

Figure \@ref(fig:gfw-kde-country-period) compares the spatial distribution of the French, British and Dutch fleets before Brexit (`r names(brexit_periods)[1]`) and after the start of the EU–UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement (`r names(brexit_periods)[2]`). The density is expressed as the share of each period's events, so the comparison is not affected by the number of years in each period or by the growth in AIS-recorded events over time. The French effort became more concentrated in the Baie de Seine after Brexit. The UK effort became slightly more diffuse and the Dutch effort slightly more concentrated in the central-eastern part of 27.7.d.

```{r gfw-kde-country-period, fig.height=8, fig.width=6, fig.cap=cap[["gfw-kde-country-period"]]}

# ---- GFW KDE by country, before and after Brexit -----------------------------------
# Density as a share of each period's events (density_share), so that the panels
# show where each fleet fishes, independent of the number of years in a period
# and of the growth in AIS-recorded events over time.

# Countries (kde_flags) and periods (brexit_periods) are set in the setup chunk

# ---- Events in the study area for the selected flags --------------------------
# Flag from vessel_meta, as in the other GFW chunks
events_study <- events_classified_fr |>
  dplyr::select(-any_of(c("vessel_flag", "vessel_name"))) |>
  left_join(vessel_meta |> dplyr::select(vesselId, vessel_flag), by = "vesselId") |>
  mutate(year = as.integer(lubridate::year(start))) |>
  filter(division    %in% study_divisions_gfw,
         vessel_flag %in% kde_flags,
         year        %in% unlist(brexit_periods))

# msg("KDE by period: ", nrow(events_study), " events after filtering")

# Project to UTM 30N
events_study_sf <- events_study |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326) |>
  st_transform(crs_proj)

# ---- KDE per period x flag, all years within a period pooled -------------------
kde_list   <- list()
kde_counts <- list()

for (period in names(brexit_periods)) {
  for (flag in kde_flags) {

    yrs <- brexit_periods[[period]]
    pts <- events_study_sf |>
      filter(vessel_flag == flag,
             year        %in% yrs)

    if (nrow(pts) < 20) {
      msg("KDE by period: ", period, " ", flag, ": only ", nrow(pts), " events, skipped")
      next
    }

    coords  <- st_coordinates(pts)
    ppp_obj <- spatstat.geom::ppp(
      x      = coords[, 1],
      y      = coords[, 2],
      window = study_owin            # points outside the window are dropped
    )
    n_points <- spatstat.geom::npoints(ppp_obj)   # events inside the study window

    kde_raw <- spatstat.explore::density.ppp(
      ppp_obj,
      sigma    = sigma_all,
      dimyx    = c(200, 200),
      positive = TRUE
    )

    kde_list[[paste(period, flag)]] <- as.data.frame(kde_raw) |>
      rename(density = value) |>
      mutate(period        = period,
             vessel_flag   = flag,
             # share of the period's events per unit area (sums to 1 over the area)
             density_share = density / n_points)

    kde_counts[[paste(period, flag)]] <- tibble::tibble(
      period      = period,
      vessel_flag = flag,
      n_points    = n_points,
      n_years     = length(yrs)
    )

    msg("KDE by period: ", period, " ", flag, ": ", n_points, " events")
  }
}

kde_study_grid <- bind_rows(kde_list)
kde_n          <- bind_rows(kde_counts)

# ---- Normalise within each country (shared scale across the two periods) --------
kde_study_grid <- kde_study_grid |>
  group_by(vessel_flag) |>
  mutate(ndensity = (density_share - min(density_share, na.rm = TRUE)) /
                    (max(density_share, na.rm = TRUE) - min(density_share, na.rm = TRUE))) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(vessel_flag = factor(vessel_flag, levels = kde_flags),
         period      = factor(period,      levels = names(brexit_periods)))

# ---- Number of events per panel, as a label in the top-left corner ----------------
study_bbox <- st_bbox(study_window_proj)

kde_n_labels <- kde_n |>
  mutate(vessel_flag = factor(vessel_flag, levels = kde_flags),
         period      = factor(period,      levels = names(brexit_periods)),
         label       = paste0("n = ", format(n_points, big.mark = ","), " events"),
         x           = study_bbox[["xmin"]] + 0.02 * (study_bbox[["xmax"]] - study_bbox[["xmin"]]),
         y           = study_bbox[["ymax"]] - 0.04 * (study_bbox[["ymax"]] - study_bbox[["ymin"]]))

# ---- Plot ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
ggplot() +
  geom_tile(data = kde_study_grid,
            aes(x = x, y = y, fill = ndensity)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    option   = "inferno",
    name     = "Relative density",
    limits   = c(0, 1),
    breaks   = c(0, 0.5, 1),
    labels   = c("Low", "Mid", "High"),
    na.value = "transparent"
  ) +
  geom_sf(data = world_proj,   fill = "grey85",
          colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf(data = fao_div_proj, fill = NA,
          colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_label(data = kde_n_labels,
             aes(x = x, y = y, label = label),
             hjust = 0, vjust = 1, size = 2.6,
             fill = alpha("white", 0.8), label.size = 0) +
  coord_sf(crs  = crs_proj,
           xlim = study_bbox[c("xmin", "xmax")],
           ylim = study_bbox[c("ymin", "ymax")],
           expand = TRUE) +
  facet_grid(vessel_flag ~ period) +
  labs(
    title    = paste0("GFW: Fishing effort density by country and period",
                      " (\u03c3 = ", sigma_all / 1000, " km)"),
    subtitle = paste0(
      study_area_lab, "  \u2014  Density as share of each period's events, ",
      "normalised within each country\n",
      "Colour scale shared across periods for each country; independent of the ",
      "number of years and events per period"
    ),
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text        = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks       = element_blank(),
        legend.position  = "bottom",
        legend.key.width = unit(2, "cm"),
        strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey90"),
        strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 9))
```

### Spatial concentration of fishing effort {#concentration}

Two complementary metrics are used to quantify the spatial concentration of fishing effort across the `r cell_size/1000` km × `r cell_size/1000` km grid cells covering the study area.

The **Gini coefficient** is a standard inequality measure borrowed from economics, adapted here to quantify the unevenness of effort across grid cells. It ranges from 0 to 1: a value of 0 means fishing effort is spread perfectly uniformly across all cells; a value of 1 means all effort is concentrated in a single cell. In practice, fishing effort is always somewhat concentrated. Values above 0.7 indicate strong spatial concentration in a small number of areas, while values below 0.5 suggest a relatively dispersed fleet. A rising Gini over time indicates that the fleet is progressively concentrating in fewer locations.

The **top-10% cell share** is a more intuitive companion metric: it asks what percentage of the total annual fishing events falls within the 10% of grid cells that were most intensively fished that year. If effort were uniform, this would be exactly 10%. In practice values of 40–70% are common in concentrated fisheries, meaning that a small fraction of the available sea area absorbs the majority of fishing pressure. Together, the two metrics capture different aspects of spatial concentration: the Gini summarises the full distribution of effort, while the top-10% share focuses specifically on the most intensively exploited areas.

For all fleets combined (Figure \@ref(fig:gfw-plot-concentration)), the Gini coefficient for `r conc_area_lab` ranged from `r conc_gini_early` in `r conc_early_lab` to `r conc_gini_late` in `r conc_late_lab`. The proportion of total effort in the most-fished 10% of cells was `r conc_top10_early`% in `r conc_early_lab` and `r conc_top10_late`% in `r conc_late_lab`, with a peak of `r conc_peak_top10`% in `r conc_peak_year`. The fishing effort became more concentrated, with a slight peak around 2020 (post-Brexit access uncertainty and COVID-19) and values remaining somewhat above the pre-2018 levels.

```{r gfw-plot-concentration, fig.height=4, fig.cap=cap[["gfw-plot-concentration"]]}

# conc_data: whole study area or focus division, see conc_scope in setup
p_gini <- ggplot(conc_data, aes(x=year, y=gini)) +
  theme_bw() +
  geom_line(colour="#E15759", linewidth=1) + geom_point(colour="#E15759", size=3) +
  geom_text(aes(label=round(gini,2)), vjust=-0.8, size=2.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=study_years) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,1), labels=scales::number_format(accuracy=0.01)) +
  theme(axis.text.x=element_text(angle=90, vjust=0.5)) +
  labs(x="", y="Gini coefficient", title="Gini coefficient")

p_top10 <- ggplot(conc_data, aes(x=year, y=top10_pct)) +
  theme_bw() +
  geom_line(colour="#4E79A7", linewidth=1) + geom_point(colour="#4E79A7", size=3) +
  geom_text(aes(label=paste0(round(top10_pct,0),"%")), vjust=-0.8, size=2.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=study_years) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,100),
                     labels=scales::percent_format(scale=1)) +
  # scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,100), expand=expansion(mult=c(0,0.15)),
  #                    labels=scales::percent_format(scale=1)) +
  theme(axis.text.x=element_text(angle=90, vjust=0.5)) +
  labs(x="", y="% of total effort", title="Top-10% cell share")

p_gini + p_top10 +
  plot_annotation(
    title    = paste0("GFW: Effort concentration ", conc_area_lab, "  \u2014  ",
                      cell_size/1000, " km grid  \u2014  All fleets"),
    subtitle = "Left: Gini coefficient (0=uniform, 1=fully concentrated). Right: % effort in top-10% cells.")
```

### Limitations of effort-based concentration metrics {#conc-limits}

The spatial concentration metrics presented above are based on GFW fishing event counts, which approximate the number of vessel-days in each grid cell. This is a measure of effort intensity in time. It does not account for the area of seabed swept per fishing event. That area varies considerably between gear types and is an important dimension of fishing impact that vessel-day counts alone cannot reveal. In addition, the increase in AIS coverage over time may affect the spatial concentration metrics.

These limitations are particularly relevant for the eastern Channel. The FDI gear split in Section \@ref(effort-split) shows the contribution of flyshoot (SSC/SDN) relative to conventional otter trawl (OTB) over the `r aer_split_years_start`–`r aer_years_end` period. These two gear types have very different relationships between fishing time and seabed area contacted.

Eigaard et al. (2017) estimated trawling intensity at both surface and subsurface levels from VMS and logbook data across European waters. They found that subsurface trawling intensities are generally much lower than surface intensities. The exception is beam trawl and dredge fisheries, where surface and subsurface contact areas are approximately equal because the heavy gear penetrates the sediment consistently across the full gear width. The Channel and southern North Sea show relatively high subsurface footprints largely for this reason.

For flyshoot, the relationship between surface and subsurface disturbance is different. The surface footprint is large while the subsurface disturbance is relatively low. Long ropes are deployed and retrieved across a wide area of seabed during the encircling phase of each set. The net footrope itself contacts a considerably smaller area with limited sediment penetration. A simple comparison of vessel-days between flyshoot and otter trawl therefore understates the surface seabed area contacted per vessel-day by flyshoot, while overstating its subsurface impact relative to beam trawl.


# Channel fisheries context: literature review {#literature}

This section places the quantitative results from Section \@ref(trends) in the broader context of the Channel fisheries literature. It draws on ICES WGCSE, STECF, Ifremer, MMO and peer-reviewed sources (see Section \@ref(lit-methods) for the literature selection approach).

## Fleet composition and dominant gear types

The Channel (ICES 27.7.d/e) is one of the most diverse and intensively fished areas in Europe. The French fleet dominates total effort in the eastern Channel, contributing over 60% of total AER fishing days in most years (ICES, 2025a; Ifremer, 2025), consistent with the AER results in Figure \@ref(fig:aer-effort-country-total), which show France as the largest contributor. Bottom trawl/seine gears account for the largest share of demersal fishing effort, targeting mixed assemblages of flatfish, cephalopods and small pelagics. The Dutch flyshoot fleet expanded slightly through the 2010s (Quirijns et al., 2020), a trend also visible in the AER series (Figure \@ref(fig:aer-split-fra-nld-bars)). Belgian beam trawl effort has declined substantially since the mid-2000s under pressure from fuel costs and quota restrictions (ILVO, 2022), consistent with the low and declining Belgian effort in the beam trawl panels throughout the AER figures.

The scallop dredge fishery is concentrated in the Baie de Seine (27.7.d) and western Channel (27.7.e), dominated by the French fleet with seasonal UK participation. Scallop landings from the Baie de Seine reached a record ~48,000 t in 2024–2025 (Varenne & Foucher, 2025). MSC certification has been granted for the Baie de Saint-Brieuc fishery (2022) and the Baie de Seine fishery (2024), covering the majority of French Channel scallop production (MSC, 2024). The landings data (Figures \@ref(fig:aer-landings-top-species), \@ref(fig:aer-landings-species-country) and \@ref(fig:aer-landings-species-gear)) confirm scallops as one of the highest-tonnage species groups, dominated by the French dredge fleet.

Pot and trap fisheries targeting whelk (*Buccinum undatum*), crab and lobster are important to UK coastal communities, though the AER series shows limited representation of this segment at the fleet level. The whelk fishery in 27.7.d has grown markedly since the mid-2010s, driven by Asian export demand (MMO, 2023).

## Historical effort trends and structural change

Total fishing effort in the Channel has declined substantially since the early 2000s, consistent with EU fleet capacity reduction programmes and quota restrictions under successive CFP reforms. The AER series (`r aer_years_start`–`r aer_years_end`) shows a general downward trend in fishing days for bottom trawl/seine and beam trawl across the major countries (Figure \@ref(fig:aer-effort-gear-cat)), with the Dutch demersal trawl/seine fleet being an exception showing some growth through the 2010s before stabilising after 2020. This is consistent with Quirijns et al. (2020) and STECF (2025a).

Post-Brexit disruption from 2021 onwards has reshaped fleet access in the eastern Channel. UK licensing restrictions have reduced French, Belgian and Dutch access to UK waters in 27.7.d/e, driving spatial redistribution towards French EEZ waters (Phillipson & Symes, 2018; House of Lords, 2022). This structural shift may contribute to the changes in spatial effort patterns visible in the GFW maps (Figures \@ref(fig:gfw-plot-kde) and \@ref(fig:gfw-kde-country-period)), with effort concentrating in the southern (French EEZ) portion of 27.7.d. Post-Brexit bilateral agreements and access negotiations between the EU Member States and the UK may continue to shape fleet access patterns in the Channel.

## Stock status of key target species {#stock-status}

Table \@ref(tab:stock-status-table) summarises the assessment and advice status for the principal commercial stocks in the Channel. Stocks are grouped by the ICES working group responsible for their assessment. Note that several species caught in the Channel, particularly cephalopods, do not have formal ICES assessments or TAC-based management; these are indicated accordingly.

```{r stock-status-table, tab.id="stock-status-table", tab.cap=cap[["stock-status-table"]]}
stock_status <- readxl::read_excel(stock_status_file, sheet = "Stock status")

stock_status |>
  flextable::flextable() |>
  flextable::italic(j = 1, part = "body") |>
  flextable::merge_v(j = c(1, 2)) |>
  style_ft_plain(font_size = 7)
```

## Fisheries for squid

Squid has emerged as an increasingly important non-quota target species in the Channel and southern North Sea, particularly for the Dutch flyshoot fleet. The Dutch fleet, initially the flyshooters and more recently otter trawlers and beam trawlers, has increasingly targeted squid during winter, driven by high profitability, the need for fleet diversification, and the absence of quota restrictions. While the common squid (*Loligo vulgaris*) was once restricted to the English Channel, it is now turning up in large numbers in the southern North Sea, with Dutch fishermen fishing intensively for this species over the past five years. Brunel et al. (2025) provide a comprehensive characterisation of the Dutch squid fishery, documenting the fleet composition, seasonal and spatial dynamics of effort and landings, bycatch species composition, and stock assessment approaches for both *Loligo vulgaris* and *L. forbesii* in the Channel and southern North Sea. The English Channel has the highest long-finned squid landings in the Northeast Atlantic, making squid one of the most valuable resources exploited by demersal fisheries in this area.

Cephalopods in the Channel and southern North Sea, principally *Loligo vulgaris*, *L. forbesii*, common cuttlefish (*Sepia officinalis*) and horned octopus (*Eledone cirrhosa*), differ fundamentally from conventional fish stocks in their population dynamics (Van de Pol et al., 2025). They are semelparous, have life cycles of approximately one year, grow extremely fast and show high natural mortality, meaning annual stock size is almost entirely determined by recruitment success rather than spawning stock size. Abundance can therefore fluctuate dramatically between years in ways that make conventional MSY-based management approaches largely unsuitable. Both *Loligo* species have expanded their distribution northward into the southern North Sea in recent decades as water temperatures have risen, and survey data confirm a clear increase in their abundance since the mid-2010s. Despite their growing commercial importance, with cuttlefish and squid together representing a substantial share of the landings in the eastern Channel and southern North Sea, no formal stock assessments or TACs exist for any of these species. Van de Pol et al. (2025) conclude that cephalopods currently operate without the biological safeguards applied to quota species and recommend development of assessment methods for *L. vulgaris* and *S. officinalis*.

## Ecosystem effects and sustainability

The seabed disturbance footprint of the Channel fisheries has been studied in the context of broader European assessments. Eigaard et al. (2017) estimated trawling intensity at surface and subsurface levels from VMS and logbook data across European shelf waters. They found that the relatively high subsurface footprint in the southern North Sea, Irish Sea, Celtic Sea and the Channel is largely due to the trawling activities of beam trawl and dredge fisheries, which have similar surface and subsurface contact areas. For most other bottom trawl types, subsurface intensities are much lower than surface intensities because gear components penetrate the sediment only shallowly. This distinction between surface and subsurface disturbance is important for evaluating the relative ecological impact of different gear types operating in the Channel. Comparisons between gear types show that Danish seine (flyshoot) has a large surface footprint due to the ropes deployed during the encircling phase, but a considerably smaller subsurface footprint (Eigaard et al., 2016a,b), while beam trawl has similar surface and subsurface contact areas due to the deep penetration of tickler chains and beam shoes (Depestele et al., 2016).

Bycatch and discards in the Channel mixed fisheries remain a management concern under the EU landing obligation (in force since 2019), though exemptions for high-survival species and *de minimis* provisions have reduced the practical scope of the obligation for many fleets (ICES, 2025a). The flyshoot fishery is generally considered to have moderate bycatch rates compared to other demersal gears, though species composition of the bycatch varies considerably with area and season (Quirijns et al., 2020).

# Discussion & Synthesis {#discussion}

## Effort trends

Total fishing effort of the EU fleets in the eastern Channel changed by `r fmt_pct(eff_eu_change_pct)` between `r aer_years_start` and `r aer_years_end`. An important driver is the contraction of the French otter trawl fleet. France dominates the effort picture, with `r fmt_pct(share_fra)` of the AER fishing days in `r aer_years_start`–`r aer_uk_years_end`, against `r fmt_pct(share_gbr)` for the UK and `r fmt_pct(share_oth)` for all other countries combined. Within the bottom trawl/seine category, conventional otter trawl (OTB/OTT/PTB) accounts for `r otb_share_range`% of the fishing days and seine/flyshoot (SSC/SDN) for `r seine_share_range`%. France and the UK fish almost entirely with otter trawls, while the Dutch fleet in the Channel fishes predominantly with flyshoot gear. Although small in absolute terms, the Dutch fleet accounts for `r fmt_pct(seine_pct("NLD"))` of the seine days in the area, with France at `r fmt_pct(seine_pct("FRA"))` and the UK at `r fmt_pct(seine_pct("GBR"))`.

The effort in these analyses has been measured in fishing days, because other metrics were not consistently available. That may affect the interpretation of the effort trends shown. For example, a flyshoot haul encloses a larger area of seabed than an otter trawl, but with lighter bottom contact. Fishing days therefore do not capture differences in seabed footprint between gears. Area swept per fishing day, based on gear-specific coefficients (Eigaard et al., 2017), would be a more meaningful measure of spatial impact.

## Landings trends

Landings from the area (in volume) are dominated by `r top_species_txt`. In the Channel, roundfish and flatfish landings have declined sharply. Scallop landings increased since 2016, supported by record biomass in the Baie de Seine (Varenne & Foucher, 2025). Cuttlefish and squid landings increased over the period, but remain small relative to other landings.

## Contribution of the UK fleet

UK effort is available from the AER up to `r aer_uk_years_end`, but not for the years after, so the post-Brexit fishing pressure of UK vessels cannot be expressed in fishing days. Over `r min(combined_years)`–`r max(combined_years)`, UK and Channel Islands vessels accounted for `r uk_share_pct`% of the landings from the eastern Channel. UK and Channel Islands landings have a clearly different fishery profile: they are dominated by shellfish (whelk, scallops, cockles and crab) taken with pots and traps and dredges, whereas EU landings are dominated by pelagic fish and scallops.

## Fleets and spatial patterns

There are indications that the main fishing grounds of the national fleets in the eastern Channel have changed after Brexit. The GFW data show persistent fishing hotspots in the Pas de Calais and the Baie de Seine. Spatial concentration for all fleets combined changed from a Gini coefficient of `r conc_gini_early` in `r conc_early_lab` to `r conc_gini_late` in `r conc_late_lab`, and the share of effort in the top-10% of grid cells from `r conc_top10_early`% to `r conc_top10_late`%. Changes in spatial distribution around the time of Brexit are consistent with the altered access conditions under the Trade and Cooperation Agreement (European Commission, 2021). However, the data cannot show whether such changes result from formal licensing, informal avoidance of previously used grounds, or other factors such as changes in target species or AIS coverage.

## Use and limitations of the data sources

The AER and GFW series measure effort in fundamentally different ways (logbook declarations versus AIS-derived vessel-days) and are not comparable in absolute terms. Differences in trend between the two series are explained by improving AIS coverage over the early years of the GFW series and by the under-representation in GFW of small inshore vessels below the AIS carriage threshold. The AER therefore provides the authoritative time series of effort and landings by fleet segment, and GFW provides the spatial resolution of within-division distributions, national fishing grounds and shifts in spatial patterns. The FDI data were used only to split the AER bottom trawl/seine category by gear code. Confidentiality suppression and EU-aggregated landings precluded their use as a primary source (STECF, 2025b).

The lack of UK effort data after Brexit creates a gap in the effort analyses, as the recent trends cannot be fully compared with historical data.

All data used here are aggregated at fleet-segment and annual level, or (GFW) at the level of fishing events. They are suited to detecting structural trends, but not to assessing compliance with management measures or bilateral agreements, which would require vessel-level logbook or VMS data. The gear split does provide a quantitative baseline against which future changes in gear composition, for example in response to gear specifications in bilateral agreements, can be assessed.

# Conclusions & Recommendations {#conclusions}

## Conclusions

1. Fishing effort of the EU fleets in the eastern Channel changed by `r fmt_pct(eff_eu_change_pct)` between `r aer_years_start` and `r aer_years_end`. France has the highest effort in the area (measured in fishing days).
2. The flyshoot fishery is a small but stable component of the fisheries in the eastern Channel. The Dutch fleet is the main seine fleet.
3. The composition of the landings is changing: scallops and cephalopods are increasing and flatfish and roundfish are declining. Pelagic fish remain relatively stable and high.
4. Post-Brexit spatial restructuring is visible from 2021, with changes in the distribution of the national fleets and a modest increase in spatial concentration.
5. The combination of AER, MMO, FDI and GFW data provides a multi-source baseline to compare the different fleets in the eastern Channel and to monitor future changes in fleet composition and spatial distribution.

## Recommendations

1. **Obtain post-Brexit UK effort data.** UK effort data for `r aer_uk_years_end + 1`–2025 (fishing days, days at sea and kW-days by year, division, gear and vessel length) should be requested from the MMO, so that the UK fleet can be included in the effort trends after Brexit.
2. **Improve the gear split between otter trawl and seine.** Unsuppressed FDI data, or national logbook data by gear code, should be requested from the relevant Member States (in particular France and the Netherlands) to make the split of the AER bottom trawl/seine category more robust.
3. **Express effort as seabed footprint.** Area swept per fishing day should be quantified with gear-specific coefficients, using the ICES VMS data product, to compare the spatial impact of otter trawl and flyshoot.
4. **Update the series when new data become available.** The AER series should be extended to 2024 once the French data are published, and the UK series once the MMO publishes the 2025 data.

# Annexes

## Annex A Data sources

| Dataset | Source | Period | Role in this report |
|---------|--------|--------|---------------------|
| STECF AER | STECF 25-07 | `r min(aer_releases$aer2025$years)`–`r max(aer_releases$aer2025$years)` | Effort and landings trends, EU fleets |
| STECF AER | STECF 21-08 | `r min(aer_releases$aer2021$years)`–`r max(aer_releases$aer2021$years)` | UK fleet effort and landings up to `r aer_uk_years_end` |
| UK landings | MMO | `r min(uk_years)`–`r max(uk_years)` | UK and Channel Islands landings after `r aer_uk_years_end` |
| STECF FDI | STECF 25-10 | `r aer_split_years_start`–`r aer_years_end` | Gear-code split of AER bottom trawl/seine |
| GFW vessel registry | GFW | `r gfw_years_start`–`r max(study_years)` | Flag, gear type, GT |
| GFW Events API | GFW API v3 (gfwr 3.0) | `r gfw_years_start`–`r max(study_years)` | Spatial analysis only |
| ICES/FAO shapefiles | ICES/FAO | – | ICES division polygons |

## Annex B Supplementary tables

The tables below summarise the key data for the study area (`r study_area_lab`), covering the period `r aer_years_start`–`r aer_years_end`. The landings tables (B1–B3) combine the AER (`r aer_source_lab`) and the MMO data: UK landings up to `r aer_uk_years_end` come from the AER, from `r aer_uk_years_end + 1` onwards and for the Channel Islands (CHI) from MMO. The effort tables (B4–B7) are based on the AER (and FDI for the gear split) only; no UK effort data are available after `r aer_uk_years_end`, so GBR effort is shown as 0 from `r aer_uk_years_end + 1` onwards and the totals for those years cover EU fleets only. Values are rounded for presentation; totals may not sum exactly due to rounding. All weights in tonnes (live weight); effort in fishing days.

```{r annex-b1, tab.id="annex-b1", tab.cap=cap[["annex-b1"]], tab.lp="annex:", tab.cap.pre="Table B"}
# AER + MMO landings (landings_combined): UK after aer_uk_years_end and CHI from MMO
make_annex_table(
  df         = landings_combined |>
                 filter(sub_reg %in% study_divisions_aer,
                        year    %in% aer_years_start:aer_years_end),
  row_var    = "year",     col_var   = "country_code",
  value_var  = "live_weight_t",
  row_label  = "Year",    col_levels = unique(report_countries_combined),
  add_other  = TRUE
)
```

Selected gears: `r paste(capacity_gears, collapse=", ")`.

```{r annex-b2, tab.id="annex-b2", tab.cap=cap[["annex-b2"]], tab.lp="annex:", tab.cap.pre="Table B"}
make_annex_table(
  df         = landings_combined |>
                 filter(sub_reg       %in% study_divisions_aer,
                        gear_category %in% capacity_gears,
                        year          %in% aer_years_start:aer_years_end),
  row_var    = "year",  col_var   = "country_code",
  value_var  = "live_weight_t",
  row_label  = "Year",  col_levels = unique(report_countries_combined),
  add_other  = TRUE
)
```

Selected gears: `r paste(capacity_gears, collapse=", ")`. Species groups as defined in Section \@ref(species-groups).

```{r annex-b3, tab.id="annex-b3", tab.cap=cap[["annex-b3"]], tab.lp="annex:", tab.cap.pre="Table B"}
# AER + MMO landings; the same species groups as in the landings figures:
# species_groups_top (key-numbers chunk), all other groups as "Other"
landings_combined |>
  filter(sub_reg       %in% study_divisions_aer,
         gear_category %in% capacity_gears,
         year          %in% aer_years_start:aer_years_end) |>
  mutate(species_group = group_species_top(species_code_harm, species_name_harm)) |>
  make_annex_table(
    row_var    = "year",  col_var    = "species_group",
    value_var  = "live_weight_t",
    row_label  = "Year",  col_levels = species_groups_top,
    add_other  = TRUE     # "Other" column for all remaining groups
  )
```

Selected gears: `r paste(capacity_gears, collapse=", ")`.

```{r annex-b4, tab.id="annex-b4", tab.cap=cap[["annex-b4"]], tab.lp="annex:", tab.cap.pre="Table B"}
make_annex_table(
  df         = aer_effort_summary |>
                 filter(sub_reg       %in% study_divisions_aer,
                        gear_category %in% capacity_gears,
                        year          %in% aer_years_start:aer_years_end),
  row_var    = "year",  col_var   = "country_code",
  value_var  = "totfishdays",
  row_label  = "Year",  col_levels = report_countries_aer,
  add_other  = TRUE
)
```

Selected gears: `r paste(capacity_gears, collapse=", ")`. VL0010 and VL40XX included for completeness.

```{r annex-b5, tab.id="annex-b5", tab.cap=cap[["annex-b5"]], tab.lp="annex:", tab.cap.pre="Table B"}
make_annex_table(
  df         = aer_effort_summary |>
                 filter(sub_reg       %in% study_divisions_aer,
                        gear_category %in% capacity_gears,
                        year          %in% aer_years_start:aer_years_end,
                        !vessel_length %in% c("UNKNOWN","NK")),
  row_var    = "year",  col_var   = "vessel_length",
  value_var  = "totfishdays",
```

Based on `aer_split`, the FDI-derived disaggregation of the AER `Bottom trawl/seine` category, all countries combined. Only direct FDI splits are shown (pooled fallback rows excluded). See Section \@ref(fdi-data) for the methodology.

```{r annex-b6, tab.id="annex-b6", tab.cap=cap[["annex-b6"]], tab.lp="annex:", tab.cap.pre="Table B"}
if (!is.null(aer_split)) {
  make_annex_table(
    df         = aer_split |>
                   filter(split_source == "FDI direct",
                          year         %in% aer_split_years_start:aer_years_end),
    row_var    = "year",  col_var   = "gear_type",
    value_var  = "totfishdays_split",
    row_label  = "Year",
    col_levels = c("Bottom trawl (OTB/OTT/PTB)", "Seine (SSC/SDN)"),
    add_other  = TRUE
  )
} else {
  cat("aer_split not available.\n")
}
```

Bottom trawl/seine disaggregated into bottom trawl (OTB/OTT/PTB) and seine (SSC/SDN) using the FDI split key. Other gears shown as reported in the AER.

```{r annex-b7, tab.id="annex-b7", tab.cap=cap[["annex-b7"]], tab.lp="annex:", tab.cap.pre="Table B"}
# Years before the FDI split is available: bottom trawl/seine unsplit
pre_split_years  <- aer_years_start:(aer_split_years_start - 1)
post_split_years <- aer_split_years_start:aer_years_end

gear_order <- c("Bottom trawl/seine (unsplit)",
                "Bottom trawl (OTB/OTT/PTB)",
                "Seine (SSC/SDN)",
                setdiff(capacity_gears, "Bottom trawl/seine"))

# Block 1: before the FDI split — BTS unsplit, other gears normal
pre2013_bts <- aer_effort_summary |>
  filter(sub_reg       %in% study_divisions_aer,
         gear_category == "Bottom trawl/seine",
         year          %in% pre_split_years) |>
  group_by(year, gear_category) |>
  summarise(totfishdays = sum(totfishdays, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop") |>
  rename(gear_label = gear_category) |>
  mutate(gear_label = "Bottom trawl/seine (unsplit)")

pre2013_other <- aer_effort_summary |>
  filter(sub_reg       %in% study_divisions_aer,
         gear_category %in% capacity_gears,
         gear_category != "Bottom trawl/seine",
         year          %in% pre_split_years) |>
  group_by(year, gear_category) |>
  summarise(totfishdays = sum(totfishdays, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop") |>
  rename(gear_label = gear_category)

# Block 2: from the FDI split onwards — BTS split via FDI, other gears normal
post2013_bts <- if (!is.null(aer_split)) {
  aer_split |>
    filter(year      %in% post_split_years,
           gear_type != "Unsplit") |>
    group_by(year, gear_type) |>
    summarise(totfishdays = sum(totfishdays_split, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop") |>
    rename(gear_label = gear_type)
} else {
  aer_effort_summary |>
    filter(sub_reg       %in% study_divisions_aer,
           gear_category == "Bottom trawl/seine",
           year          %in% post_split_years) |>
    group_by(year, gear_category) |>
    summarise(totfishdays = sum(totfishdays, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop") |>
    rename(gear_label = gear_category) |>
    mutate(gear_label = "Bottom trawl/seine (unsplit)")
}

post2013_other <- aer_effort_summary |>
  filter(sub_reg       %in% study_divisions_aer,
         gear_category %in% capacity_gears,
         gear_category != "Bottom trawl/seine",
         year          %in% post_split_years) |>
  group_by(year, gear_category) |>
  summarise(totfishdays = sum(totfishdays, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop") |>
  rename(gear_label = gear_category)

all_data <- bind_rows(pre2013_bts, pre2013_other,
                      post2013_bts, post2013_other) |>
  mutate(totfishdays = round(totfishdays)) |>
  group_by(year, gear_label) |>
  summarise(totfishdays = sum(totfishdays, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from  = gear_label,
              values_from = totfishdays,
              values_fill = NA) |>
  dplyr::select(year, any_of(gear_order)) |>
  arrange(year) |>
  mutate(Total = rowSums(across(any_of(gear_order)), na.rm=TRUE))

# Build total row separately on the completed data frame
total_row <- all_data |>
  summarise(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) sum(x, na.rm=TRUE))) |>
  mutate(year = NA_integer_)

# Bind and convert year to character
all_data <- bind_rows(all_data, total_row) |>
  mutate(year = if_else(is.na(year), "Total", as.character(year)))

# Convert NA to "--" for display (must be character columns)
all_data_display <- all_data |>
  mutate(across(any_of(gear_order),
                \(x) if_else(is.na(x), "--", formatC(x, format="d", big.mark=","))))

# Rename year column
names(all_data_display)[1] <- "Year"

# Build flextable
ft <- flextable::flextable(all_data_display) |>
  style_ft(font_size = 8) |>
  # Shade the years before the FDI split slightly to signal the unsplit period
  # rows as a logical vector: a formula (~ Year %in% ...) is evaluated by
  # flextable outside this chunk's environment and cannot see pre_split_years
  flextable::bg(i = all_data_display$Year %in% as.character(pre_split_years),
                j = c("Bottom trawl (OTB/OTT/PTB)", "Seine (SSC/SDN)"),
                bg = "#EEEEEE")

ft
```
